blocks.tk: Türkmen dili türki dilleriň oguz toparyna degişli. Ol Türkmenistanyň döwlet dili. Türkmenistandan başga-da, bu dilde Eýranyň we Owganystanyň demirgazygynda, Özbegistanda, Täjigistanda we Russiýada ýaşaýan türkmenler gürleýärler. Çeşmelere görä, türkmen dilinde ýedi million töweregi adam gürleýär.
blocks.en: Turkmen belongs to the Oghuz branch of the Turkic languages and is the state language of Turkmenistan. Outside Turkmenistan it is spoken by Turkmen in northern Iran and northern Afghanistan, in Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, and in Russia's Stavropol region. Counts vary: Wikipedia, citing Ethnologue, gives about 6.8 million native speakers, and a 2023 study by the linguist Sema Aslan Demir more than seven million.

blocks.tk: Türkmen diliniň birnäçe şiwesi bar. Olaryň köpüsiniň ady taýpalaryň adyndan gelýär: Teke, Ýomut, Ärsary, Salyr, Saryk, Gökleň, Çowdur we başgalar. Her şiwede, esasan, şol taýpanyň ýaşaýan ýerlerinde gürleýärler. Edebi dil, ýagny mekdeplerde okadylýan we kitaplarda ulanylýan dil, esasan Teke şiwesine esaslanýar. Eýrandaky türkmenleriň köpüsi Ýomut, Owganystandakylar bolsa Ärsary şiwesinde gürleýärler.
blocks.en: Turkmen has several dialects, and most are named after the tribes whose members speak them. Larry Clark's grammar, as summarized in the Encyclopaedia Iranica, lists ten main groups: Teke (with its Ahal and Mary varieties), Yomut, Ersary, Salyr, Saryk, Chowdur, Alili, Göklen, Nohur and Änew. The standard language, the one taught in schools and used in print, is based mainly on Teke. According to Wikipedia, most Turkmen in Iran speak Yomut, and most in Afghanistan speak Ersary.

blocks.tk: Türkmen dilinde uzyn we gysga çekimliler bar. Ýazuwda olar görkezilmeýär, ýöne sözüň manysyny üýtgedýär. Adam ady manysyndaky at sözünde a uzyn aýdylýar, haýwan manysyndaky at sözünde bolsa gysga. Ot sözi hem ýangyn manysynda uzyn, ösümlik manysynda gysga aýdylýar. Teke, Ýomut we Gökleň şiwelerinde s we z sesleri dil bilen dişleriň arasynda aýdylýar. Gepleşikde o ýa-da u bar bolan sözlerde indiki a hem köplenç o ýaly eşidilýär: gulak sözi gulok ýaly aýdylýar.
blocks.en: Turkmen has long and short vowels. Writing doesn't mark them, but they change meaning: at, a name, is said with a long a, and at, a horse, with a short one; ot is fire when the o is long and grass when it is short. The Encyclopaedia Iranica counts the long vowels among the language's most archaic features. In the Teke, Yomut and Göklen dialects, s and z are said with the tongue between the teeth, like the th of English thin and this, while Chowdur, Nohur and some others keep a plain s and z, Aslan Demir notes. The same study adds that in speech the vowel after an o or a u is often rounded too: gulak, ear, sounds closer to gulok.

blocks.tk: Türkmen dilinde ýazylan edebiýatyň taryhy 14-nji asyra çenli gidýär. Uzak wagtlap türkmen şahyrlary Orta Aziýanyň köp halkynyň umumy edebi dili bolan çagataý dilinde ýazypdyrlar. 18-nji we 19-njy asyrlarda bolsa türkmenleriň öz edebi dili döräp başlapdyr. Magtymguly şol döwrüň iň meşhur şahyry: oňa türkmen edebiýatynyň atasy diýýärler.
blocks.en: Turkmen writing has a literary tradition going back to the 14th century, according to Britannica. For a long time Turkmen poets wrote in Chagatai, a literary language shared by many peoples of Central Asia; a literary language of the Turkmen's own began to emerge in the 18th and 19th centuries. Its best-known poet of that time is Magtymguly, whom Wikipedia calls the father of Turkmen literature.

blocks.tk: Türkmenler köp asyrlap arap elipbiýinde ýazypdyrlar. Ilkinji türkmen elipbiý kitaby 1913-nji ýylda, ilkinji türkmen gazeti bolsa 1914-nji ýylda çykypdyr. 1920-nji ýyllaryň ahyrynda arap elipbiýiniň ýerine latyn elipbiýi, 1940-njy ýylda bolsa kiril elipbiýi girizildi. Türkmenistan garaşsyzlygyny alandan soň, 1993-nji ýylda täze latyn elipbiýi kabul edildi, 1999-njy ýylda bolsa onuň käbir harplary üýtgedildi. Häzirki elipbiýde 30 harp bar, olaryň arasynda ä, ç, ž, ň, ö, ş, ü we ý harplary hem bar. Eýranda we Owganystanda ýaşaýan türkmenler bolsa häzir hem arap elipbiýini ulanýarlar.
blocks.en: For centuries Turkmen was written in the Arabic script. According to Wikipedia, the first Turkmen primer appeared in 1913 and the first newspaper in 1914. In the late 1920s a Latin alphabet replaced the Arabic one (Wikipedia dates its approval to 3 January 1928, Britannica gives 1927), and in 1940 Cyrillic replaced the Latin. After independence, the parliament adopted a new Latin alphabet on 12 April 1993; in 1999 some of its letters, such as $, £ and ¥, were replaced by ş, ž and ý. Today's alphabet has 30 letters, among them ä, ç, ž, ň, ö, ş, ü and ý. Turkmen in Iran and Afghanistan still write in the Arabic script.

blocks.title: Reading the Turkmen
blocks.text: Look for this unit's grammar: the causatives *okadylýan* (taught, from *okatmak* with the passive), *girizildi* (was brought in, from *girmek*) and *üýtgedýär* (changes, from *üýtgemek*), with the soft *t* turning into *d* before a vowel or *-ýär*. *Ýagny* means **that is**.

sources.title: Turkmen language
sources.note: About 6.8 million native speakers (citing Ethnologue); where it is spoken; the standard based on Teke, Iranian Turkmen mostly speaking Yomut and Afghan Turkmen Ersary; the first primer (1913) and newspaper (1914); the Latin alphabet approved on 3 January 1928, Cyrillic from 1940, the new Latin alphabet approved by the Mejlis on 12 April 1993; Magtymguly as the father of Turkmen literature.

sources.title: Turkmen alphabet
sources.note: The symbols £, $, ¢, ¥ and ÿ of the 1993 alphabet replaced in 1999 by ž, ş and ý (citing the Institute of the Estonian Language); 30 letters; the Arabic script used in Iran and Afghanistan.

sources.title: Turkmen language
sources.note: The southwestern (Oghuz) branch of the Turkic languages; a literary tradition from the 14th century, then the Chagatai literary language, and a Turkmen literary language emerging in the 18th and 19th centuries; the Latin alphabet adopted in 1927, Cyrillic in 1940, Latin again after independence.

sources.title: Turkmens of Persia ii. Language
sources.note: Clark's list of the main dialects (Teke with Ahal and Mary, Yomut, Ersary, Salyr, Saryk, Chowdur, Alili, Göklen, Nohur, Änew); the dialects tied to the areas where each tribe lives; the preservation of long vowels as an archaic feature.

sources.title: Spoken Turkmen
sources.publisher: S. Aslan Demir, Journal of Endangered Languages 13 (23), 2023, on DergiPark
sources.note: More than seven million speakers; the standard based on Teke; long vowels in root syllables that change meaning; interdental s and z in Teke, Yomut, Göklen and related varieties, dental in Chowdur and Nohur; rounding of the next vowel in speech (gulak said as gulok).
